Jean Morel
zhahn mo-rel'
n. (Jean Morel, d. 1574, Huguenot pastor and correspondent of Calvin)
French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Morel, from Old French more, dark, swarthy.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jean Morel, lord of Collonges, was one of the pastors sent out of Geneva into the French churches in the years when those churches were being organised under persecution, and his correspondence with Calvin is part of the record of how that was done. The letters are not devotional: they are about where a minister can be placed, which congregation can pay, who has been arrested, whether a man of doubtful soundness should be received, how a church without a building should hold the Supper. The dictionary gives him an entry for the sake of that correspondence. The French Reformed church of the 1550s and 1560s was built by letter, under a government that would have hanged everyone named in them, and the men who wrote and carried those letters took the same risk as the men who preached. The ordinary administration of a persecuted church is one of the most unremembered forms of courage, and Morel's letters preserve its texture better than any martyrology.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines correspondence as intercourse by letters, and courier as a messenger sent in haste.

expand to see more

CORRESPOND'ENCE, n. Intercourse between persons at a distance, by means of letters sent and answers received.

COU'RIER, n. A messenger sent express with letters or dispatches.

CLAN'DESTINE, a. Secret; private; hidden; withdrawn from public view.

ADMINISTRA'TION, n. The executive part of government; the management of any office or employment.

Modern Corruption

His letters to Calvin are the working record of how a hunted church was organised and supplied with pastors.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a romance about the underground church that remembers only its heroics. The letters show the actual work: stipends, placements, bad candidates, arrests, and the slow business of getting a minister to a town that had asked for one. It was dangerous and it was clerical, and both words are true at once.

The principle to recover is that the New Testament is itself full of this traffic and names the men who carried it. Tychicus is sent so that the church may know Paul's state: “who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord” (Col 4:7). Onesimus is sent back by hand — “Whom I have sent again” (Phm 1:12). Those who receive and forward such messengers share in the work: “We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth” (3Jo 1:8). And the apostle names his fellow labourers one by one — “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” (Rom 16:3).

Usage

"“a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord” (Col 4:7) — pastors placed in France by letter from Geneva."

"“fellowhelpers to the truth” (3Jo 1:8) — stipends, lodgings and the Supper without a building."

"“Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” (Rom 16:3) — a correspondence that could have hanged everyone in it."
